Claudius. King of Denmark. He is the regicidal uncle who murders his brother, Prince Hamlet's father, with poison. He marries the dead king's widow Gertrude and usurps the throne—all with a veneer of legitimate succession. When his crime is revealed by his brother's ghost, Claudius becomes a man of conscience, able to pray but unable to repent. He says, "Words without thoughts never to heaven go." Yet he is too entrenched in power to undo the deed. His attempt to silence the investigation leads him to manipulate Hamlet, arrange Hamlet's execution, and ultimately engineer the deaths of nearly every character in the play.

Claudius pours poison into his sleeping brother's ear, a murder so foul it horrifies even the ghost. He acts both from ambition—desire for the throne—and lust for Gertrude, whom he immediately marries after the funeral. The murder is so recent that the court is still mourning when Claudius is crowned king. His swiftness suggests planning.

Claudius presents himself as a capable ruler who has stabilized the kingdom. Denmark faces external threats from Fortinbras of Norway. He speaks eloquently at court, appearing merciful and reasonable. He grants Hamlet the right to remain at Elsinore rather than return to Wittenberg and attempts to befriend him. His marriage to Gertrude is described by Hamlet as incestuous sheets—it was incestuous under canon law to marry a widow of one's brother. This suggests Claudius has manipulated Gertrude into complicity.

Hamlet encounters his father's ghost, who reveals the murder and demands vengeance. Hamlet feigns madness to investigate the truth. Claudius, watching Hamlet's erratic behavior, grows increasingly suspicious and paranoid. When a travelling troupe of players arrives, Hamlet arranges to have them perform a play mirroring the murder called The Mousetrap. Claudius's reaction during the poisoning scene confirms the crime.

Claudius, now certain that Hamlet knows his secret, arranges for Hamlet to be sent to England with orders to execute him. Hamlet switches the orders and returns. Claudius sets up a duel between Hamlet and Laertes, Ophelia's brother, poisoning Laertes' sword and preparing a poisoned drink as backup. The plan backfires. The poisoned sword and drink kill Gertrude, Laertes, Hamlet, and Claudius himself. His guilt and betrayal destroy the entire court.

In a soliloquy, Claudius reveals that he cannot repent. He still desires the throne and Gertrude, and repentance would require surrendering both. He says, "I am still possessed of those effects for which I did the murder." Yet he is tormented by prayer and guilt, a man conscious of his damnation but unable to change course.
